title: Persistent catatonia following epileptic seizures: a case report and systematic literature search
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old man with known epilepsy, who had discontinued his antiepileptic drugs, was brought to the emergency department after being found in the street confused and amnestic. History was limited by bradyphrenia and amnesia; he had no psychiatric history.  
In the emergency department:  
• Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.  
• Urine toxicology screen was negative.  
• Noncontrast CT of the brain and CSF analysis (cells and protein) were normal.  
• Blood tests showed a slight leukocytosis.  
• EEG revealed generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges.  

He was admitted to neurology for further evaluation. On hospital day 2, he reported having fallen during what he believed was a generalized tonic–clonic seizure and acknowledged nonadherence to his antiepileptic drugs; valproic acid was restarted at 1500 mg/day. Repeat labs showed a decreased leukocytosis, creatine kinase of 521 U/L, and C-reactive protein of 16.2 mg/L. Brain MRI was normal.  

On hospital day 4, nursing staff witnessed a generalized tonic–clonic seizure; valproic acid was increased to 2000 mg/day. EEG remained unchanged. Subsequently, the patient became bradyphrenic, spoke minimally, and maintained a fixed stare, prompting psychiatric consultation. Mental status examination showed clear consciousness, flat affect, intact orientation, normal attention, and no perceptual disturbances. Initial assessment noted insufficient DSM-5 criteria for catatonia.  

Three days later, he exhibited hand-rubbing stereotypies, grimacing, sustained posturing, and ambitendency. The Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score was 12. A repeat EEG remained without epileptiform activity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered psychogenic non‐epileptic seizure vs true epileptic seizure — “we detected however, after the first and second seizures, … a substantial increase in CK which, according to experts, could be a diagnostic instrument for differentiating between ES and PNES”  
2. Considered side effects of valproic acid — “the differential diagnosis at that stage included side effects of the valproic acid” — excluded since “when the AEDs were restarted, the catatonia did not go into remission, and only did so when we augmented the lorazepam to 17 mg/d”  
3. Considered postictal delirium — excluded because “our observation that the patient remained well-oriented and attentive argued against delirium”  
4. Considered postictal psychosis — excluded because “except for the psychomotor symptoms, there were no other symptoms of psychosis” and there were no delusions or hallucinations  
5. Considered nonconvulsive status epilepticus — excluded because “repetitive EEGs showing no signs of epileptic activity”
